regions.name: Duchy of Württemberg
regions.note: Raised to a duchy at the Diet of Worms (1495). Under Habsburg administration 1520–1534 after Duke Ulrich was expelled; Protestant from 1534. The exclave of Montbéliard (Mömpelgard) and small holdings are left out. Became an electorate in 1803, shown by the border data from then.

regions.name: Margraviate of Baden-Durlach
regions.note: The Protestant (Ernestine) half of Baden after the division of 1535: the lower margraviate around Pforzheim and Durlach and the upper lands of Hachberg, Rötteln and Badenweiler in the Breisgau (two pieces). Charles William founded Karlsruhe in 1715. Reunited with Baden-Baden in 1771.

regions.name: Margraviate of Baden-Durlach
regions.note: The Protestant (Ernestine) half of Baden after the division of 1535: the lower margraviate around Pforzheim and Durlach and the upper lands of Hachberg, Rötteln and Badenweiler in the Breisgau (two pieces). Charles William founded Karlsruhe in 1715. Reunited with Baden-Baden in 1771.

regions.name: Margraviate of Baden-Baden
regions.note: The Catholic (Bernhardine) half of Baden after the division of 1535, on the Rhine plain and northern Black Forest around Baden-Baden and Rastatt (its Spanheim and Luxembourg holdings are left out). Passed to Baden-Durlach when August George died in 1771.

regions.name: Margraviate of Baden
regions.note: Baden reunited under Charles Frederick of Baden-Durlach in 1772 after the Baden-Baden line died out (1771). Made an electorate in 1803, from when the border data shows it.

regions.name: Principality of Ansbach
regions.note: The Franconian Hohenzollern principality 'below the mountains' (Brandenburg-Ansbach), separated from Bayreuth in 1486. Charles Alexander sold it to Prussia in 1791; Bavaria took it in 1806. Its many small exclaves are smoothed.

regions.name: Principality of Bayreuth
regions.note: The Franconian Hohenzollern principality 'above the mountains' (Brandenburg-Kulmbach, later Brandenburg-Bayreuth) around Kulmbach, Bayreuth and Hof, separated from Ansbach in 1486. Its lower district around Erlangen and Neustadt an der Aisch is left out. Passed to Prussia with Ansbach in 1791.

regions.name: Free Imperial City of Nuremberg
regions.note: Nuremberg, a free imperial city from 1219, bought the burgraves' rights in 1427 and won the largest territory of any imperial city (Lauf, Hersbruck, Altdorf) in the Landshut War of Succession in 1504–1505. Drawn from 1505 to 1796, when Prussia occupied its outer districts; annexed by Bavaria in 1806.

regions.name: Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg
regions.note: The ecclesiastical principality of the archbishops of Salzburg in the Salzach valley (Pongau, Pinzgau, Lungau), which became fully separate from Bavaria with its own territorial law in 1328. Rich from salt and gold; it expelled its Protestants in 1731. Secularised in 1803 (the border data's 'Electorate of Salzburg'). Berchtesgaden, a separate provostry, is left out of the outline only roughly.

regions.name: Margraviate of Meissen
regions.note: The march on the middle Elbe held by the House of Wettin from 1089 (silver found at Freiberg in 1168 made it rich). Henry the Illustrious added Thuringia in 1247 (not drawn here). When Frederick the Warlike received the Saxon electorate in 1423 the Wettin lands became 'Saxony'; the border data's 'Electorate of Saxony' shows them from then.

regions.name: Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg
regions.note: The Ascanian duchy of Saxony around Wittenberg on the middle Elbe, split from Saxe-Lauenburg in 1296; the Golden Bull (1356) made its duke an elector. When the line died out in 1422 Emperor Sigismund gave it to the Wettin margrave of Meissen.

regions.name: Duchy of Pomerania
regions.note: The Griffin dukes' Pomerania on the Baltic from the Recknitz to the Łeba, a fief of the Empire from 1181. The second slice adds Rügen (inherited 1325) and the eastern lands of Schlawe and Stolp. Partitioned among lines (Stettin, Wolgast) for most of its history. When Bogislaw XIV died in 1637 it was occupied by Sweden and divided with Brandenburg in 1648. The region runs east of 15°E; the border data shows it as minor states.

rulers.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower, then Lucius D. Clay (US)

regions.note: Germany west of the Oder–Neisse line after the surrender of May 1945, divided into American, British, French and Soviet zones under the Allied Control Council. The western zones became the Federal Republic in May 1949 and the Soviet zone the German Democratic Republic in October 1949. Berlin, under four-power rule, lies inside the Soviet zone outline; the American enclave of Bremen is part of the British zone here. The Saar was split from the French zone in 1947 (separate entry). The border data colours the zones as the United States and the Soviet Union.

regions.name: Saar Protectorate
regions.note: The Saar, detached from the French zone in 1947 as a protectorate with its own constitution and government in customs and currency union with France. After voters rejected the European statute in the 1955 referendum it joined West Germany on 1 January 1957. Drawn at its 1947–1956 borders, simplified; the border data colours it French.

regions.name: Signoria of Milan
regions.note: The lordship over Milan, held by the della Torre from 1259 and by the Visconti after Archbishop Ottone's victory at Desio (1277); the della Torre returned in 1302–1311. Under Azzone and his successors it spread over most of Lombardy (Bergamo, Brescia, Cremona, Pavia, Novara, Piacenza, Parma by 1346; second slice). Gian Galeazzo took Verona and Vicenza in 1387 (third slice) and bought the ducal title in 1395. Extents are approximate; Mantua stays outside.

regions.name: Duchy of Milan
regions.note: Gian Galeazzo Visconti bought the title of duke from King Wenceslaus in 1395; by his death in 1402 he also held Pisa, Siena, Perugia and Bologna (not drawn). The border data shows the Duchy of Milan from 1402.

regions.name: Lordship of Mantua
regions.note: The Gonzaga state of Mantua: a lordship (capitanato) from Luigi Gonzaga's coup of 1328, a marquisate from 1433 and a duchy from 1530. After the War of the Mantuan Succession (1628–1631) it passed to the Gonzaga-Nevers; Austria annexed it in 1708 when Ferdinando Carlo sided with France. The border data shows the area as minor states.

regions.name: Lordship of Ferrara (Este)
regions.note: The lands of the House of Este: Ferrara, a papal fief, from Obizzo II's acclamation as perpetual lord in 1264, and the imperial fiefs of Modena (1288) and Reggio (1289; lost 1306–1409), with the Garfagnana from 1429. Ferrara was a duchy from 1471. When Alfonso II died without a legitimate heir in 1597 the pope took Ferrara back and the Este kept Modena and Reggio. The border data puts Ferrara in the Papal States.

regions.name: Republic of Siena
regions.note: The commune of Siena and its contado over southern Tuscany (Montalcino, Grosseto, Massa Marittima, the Maremma coast to Talamone). Visconti lordship 1399–1404 and Spanish garrisons in the 1540s; after the siege of 1554–1555 Siena surrendered to Charles V's forces, and in 1557 it was granted to Cosimo de' Medici. Drawn from 1200 (commune from 1125 per Wikidata).

regions.name: Republic of Lucca
regions.note: The city-republic of Lucca with its contado and part of the Garfagnana, independent from the 12th century (Wikidata 1160) until the French made it the Principality of Lucca and Piombino in 1805. Under Castruccio Castracani (1316–1328) it briefly ruled much of western Tuscany (not drawn). Drawn to 1799; the border data puts it in Tuscany from 1800.

regions.name: Duchy of Lucca
regions.note: Created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 for the Bourbon-Parma heirs; Charles Louis ceded it to Tuscany in 1847, a year before he inherited Parma. Drawn on the old republic's outline; the border data shows Tuscany here.

regions.name: Duchy of Urbino
regions.note: The Montefeltro and della Rovere duchy in the northern Marche (Urbino, Gubbio, Cagli, Fossombrone, San Leo), a papal fief ruled as an independent court, famed under Federico da Montefeltro. Pesaro and Senigallia were added from 1513 (second slice). Devolved to the Papal States in 1631. Drawn from 1443, when Oddantonio da Montefeltro was made duke; San Marino lies within the outline.

regions.name: Duchy of Gaeta
regions.note: A small coastal duchy between Rome and Naples, nominally Byzantine, independent under the Docibilian dynasty from the 9th century; from 1032 it was held by Lombard and then Norman lords and in 1140 was absorbed into Roger II's Kingdom of Sicily. Extent (Gaeta, Fondi, Traetto, the lower Garigliano) approximate.

regions.name: Lordship, later Principality of Piombino
regions.note: A small coastal state facing Elba, founded when Gherardo Appiani sold Pisa to the Visconti in 1399 and kept Piombino; a principality from 1594. Elba (drawn as a second piece) belonged to it except Portoferraio, Medici from 1548. Ceded to France in 1801 and given to Elisa Bonaparte in 1805.

regions.name: Duchy of Montferrat
regions.note: The old marquisate of Montferrat, held by the Gonzaga of Mantua from 1536 and raised to a duchy in 1574. Savoy took part of it after the War of the Mantuan Succession (Treaty of Cherasco, 1631) and the rest in 1708. Upper and lower Montferrat are drawn as one simplified piece; the border data shows Spanish Milan here.

regions.name: Free Territory of Trieste
regions.note: The free territory created by the 1947 peace treaty with Italy, never given its UN governor: Zone A (Trieste) was run by British and American forces, Zone B (Koper, Buje) by Yugoslavia. The 1954 London Memorandum gave Zone A to Italy and Zone B to Yugoslavia. The border data shows the whole area as Yugoslavia.

title: Middle East: states the border data lacks, 2400 BCE–1886
summary: Cliopatria's borders leave out many states of Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Arabia, Iran and the South Caucasus. This layer adds 76 of them: Bronze and Iron Age kingdoms (Ebla, Mari, Yamhad, Kizzuwatna, Arzawa, Ugarit, Aram-Damascus, Ammon, Moab, Edom, Mannaea), the city-kingdoms of Cyprus, Characene, Elymais, Hatra, Kinda and Muhammad's state at Medina; the Caucasian kingdoms and emirates of the 9th–12th centuries (Tbilisi, Lori, Kakheti-Hereti, Syunik, Kars) and the dynasties of the 'Iranian intermezzo' (Sallarids, Rawwadids, Hasanwayhids, Kakuyids, Marwanids, Uqaylids, Mirdasids, Mazyadids, Ikhshidids); the Burids of Damascus, the Nizari Ismaili castles, the atabegs of Azerbaijan, Fars, Luristan and Kerman; the eastern Anatolian beyliks (Saltukids, Mengujekids, Shah-Armens, Artuqids, Eretnids, Kadi Burhan al-Din, Erzincan, Tacettin, Lâdik, Alaiye); the Mamluk pashas of Baghdad; Arabian states from the Sulayhids to the Jabrids, Bani Khalid, Kathiri, Mahra and Lahej; and the South Caucasus khanates of 1747–1828, which replace the border data's single 'Khanates of the Caucasus'. Dates and capitals come from cited reference articles; borders are reconstructions checked against Shepherd's Historical Atlas and the descriptions in those articles. Few pre-modern sources describe frontiers, so every line here is approximate.

regions.name: Ebla
regions.note: The first Eblaite kingdom of the archive period (Royal Palace G), the dominant power of north-western Syria until its destruction c. 2300 BCE, attributed to Sargon or Naram-Sin of Akkad. The archive names many dependent towns; the extent (Amuq to the Euphrates bend at Emar, south to Hama) follows the usual modern reading and is approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ebla'.

regions.name: Mari (Lim dynasty)
regions.note: The Amorite Lim dynasty of Mari controlled the middle Euphrates from Terqa to the Suhum border and the lower Khabur. Between the two slices Mari was held by Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia (his son Yasmah-Addu as king); Hammurabi of Babylon conquered Zimri-Lim in 1761 and destroyed the city c. 1759 BCE. Middle chronology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mari, Syria'.

regions.name: Mari (Lim dynasty)

regions.name: Yamhad
regions.note: Amorite kingdom centred on Halab (Aleppo), the leading Syrian power of the 18th century BCE (Yarim-Lim I and Hammurabi I had some twenty vassal kings). Only the core realm is drawn, from the Amuq to the Euphrates bend and south to the Qatna frontier; vassals such as Alalakh lie inside. Ended by the Hittite conquests of Hattusili I and Mursili I (Aleppo destroyed c. 1600/1595 BCE). Middle chronology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Yamhad'.

regions.name: Kizzuwatna
regions.note: Kingdom of the Cilician plain and the Anti-Taurus up to Kummanni (Comana), independent between the Hittite Old and New Kingdoms and alternately allied to Hatti and Mitanni; absorbed by the Hittites in the early 14th century BCE. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kizzuwatna'.

regions.name: Arzawa
regions.note: Arzawa Minor, the chief state of the Arzawa lands of western Anatolia, with its capital at Apasa (Ephesus); its king Tarhundaradu corresponded with Amenhotep III. Mursili II conquered it c. 1320 BCE and divided it into the vassal kingdoms of Mira, Hapalla and the Seha River Land. The extent (Hermus to the Maeander, inland to the Lakes) is approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Arzawa'.

regions.name: Ugarit
regions.note: Coastal kingdom of Ras Shamra between Mount Casius (Jebel Aqra) and the Siyannu border, a vassal first of Egypt and from c. 1350 BCE of the Hittites, but ruled by its own dynasty until its destruction c. 1185 BCE. Area about 2,000 km²; the inland border is approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ugarit'.

regions.name: Bit Adini
regions.note: Aramaean kingdom on both banks of the Euphrates below Carchemish, with its capital at Til Barsip (Tell Ahmar); Shalmaneser III of Assyria took it from Ahuni in 856 BCE and renamed the capital Kar-Shalmaneser. Carchemish (drawn by the border data among the Neo-Hittite states) is left outside. Sources: Wikipedia 'Bit Adini'.

regions.name: Aram-Damascus
regions.note: Aramaean kingdom of Damascus and the Hauran. Under Hazael (c. 842–796 BCE) it dominated Israel and took Gilead and Bashan; the middle slice extends to the Jabbok. Tiglath-Pileser III annexed it in 732 BCE. Sources: Wikipedia 'Aram-Damascus'; Shepherd plate 5 (750–625 BCE).

regions.name: Aram-Damascus

regions.name: Ammon
regions.note: Kingdom east of the Jordan between the Jabbok and the Arnon around Rabbath Ammon (Amman); an Assyrian tributary from 734 BCE, absorbed after the Babylonian campaign of 582 BCE. The frontier with Moab moved repeatedly; the line here is a compromise. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ammon'.

regions.name: Moab
regions.note: Kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon/Madaba plains and the Zered (Wadi Hasa); King Mesha's stele (c. 840 BCE) records its revolt from Israel and expansion north of the Arnon. An Assyrian tributary from 734 BCE; conquered by Nebuchadnezzar II in 582 BCE. Start date approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Moab'.

regions.name: Edom
regions.note: Kingdom south of the Zered as far as the Gulf of Aqaba, with its capital at Bozrah (Busayra); it broke from Judah in the mid-9th century BCE, paid tribute to Assyria from 734, and fell to Nabonidus of Babylon c. 552 BCE. The western border on the Arabah is approximate; later Edomite expansion into the Negev is not drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Edom'; Shepherd plate 5.

regions.name: Mannaea
regions.note: Kingdom south and south-east of Lake Urmia (capital probably Izirtu, near Saqqez), a buffer between Urartu and Assyria; absorbed by the Medes after 616 BCE. Extent approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mannaea'.

regions.name: Marion
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. The island-wide division into kingdoms is a modern reconstruction from the location of the capitals, sanctuaries and the main valleys; no ancient source gives frontiers, so every line is conjectural. Start date simplified to 600 BCE (after the end of Assyrian domination in 609). Sources: Wikipedia 'Ancient history of Cyprus' and the city's article; Shepherd plate 5.

regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. Sold to Kition in the 340s BCE, then given to Salamis by Alexander (332 BCE).

regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. regions.name: Kition
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. Kition (Phoenician dynasty) annexed Idalion c. 450 BCE and bought Tamassos in the 340s; Alexander gave Tamassos to Pnytagoras of Salamis (332 BCE). Slices follow those changes, with approximate dates.

The leading kingdom; Evagoras I briefly united most of the island (c. 391–380 BCE), not drawn. The separate Tamassos piece (332–312 BCE) was Alexander's gift to Salamis.

regions.name: Salamis (Tamassos)
regions.note: One of the city-kingdoms of Iron Age Cyprus, listed (with nine others) on the Prism of Esarhaddon (673 BCE) or attested on Persian-period coins; tributary in turn to Assyria, Egypt (c. 570–545 BCE) and the Achaemenids, but ruled by its own kings until Ptolemy I abolished the kingdoms in 312–310 BCE. regions.name: Characene
regions.note: Kingdom at the head of the Persian Gulf founded by Hyspaosines after the Seleucid collapse; capital Charax Spasinou. Frequently a Parthian vassal but with its own kings and coinage until Ardashir I annexed it c. 222. Drawn over the Parthian outline. Sources: Wikipedia 'Characene'.

regions.name: Elymais
regions.capital: Seleucia on the Hedyphon; Susa at times
regions.note: Autonomous kingdom in the Zagros foothills of Khuzestan (Susiana), often a Parthian vassal; held Susa at times. Conquered by Ardashir I c. 221. Extent approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Elymais'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Araba (Hatra)
regions.note: Arab kingdom of the caravan city of Hatra in the Jazira steppe, under Parthian suzerainty; its rulers took the title 'king of the Arabs' from the mid-2nd century. It repelled Trajan (117) and Septimius Severus (198/199) and fell to the Sasanian Shapur I in 240/241. Only the steppe around the city is drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hatra' and 'Kingdom of Hatra'.

regions.name: Kindah Kingdom
regions.note: Hujrid kings of Kinda ruled the Ma'add tribes of north and central Arabia c. 450–550, as clients of Himyar; their power collapsed after al-Harith ibn Amr's death in 528. The area drawn (Najd and al-Yamama) is a rough indication of tribal hegemony, not a frontier. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kinda'.

regions.name: First Islamic state (Medina)
regions.note: The polity Muhammad founded at Medina in 622 under the Constitution of Medina. Slices: the Medina oasis (622–627); after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya and the conquest of Khaybar (628–629); after the conquest of Mecca (630), Hunayn and Ta'if, most of the Hejaz, Tihama and western Najd (630–632). The many deputations of 630–631 brought looser allegiances from the rest of Arabia, not drawn. Succeeded by the Rashidun Caliphate (drawn by the border data from 633). Sources: Wikipedia 'First Islamic state' and 'Constitution of Medina'.

regions.name: Emirate of Tbilisi
regions.note: Arab emirate based in Tbilisi from 736; effectively independent of the caliphate from the 830s (Ishaq ibn Ismail, crushed by Bugha al-Kabir in 853), later a city-state ruled by its emirs and then a council of elders until David IV of Georgia took it in 1122. The first slice covers central Kartli, the second only the city's district. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Tbilisi'.

regions.name: Emirate of Tbilisi
regions.note: Arab emirate based in Tbilisi from 736; effectively independent of the caliphate from the 830s (Ishaq ibn Ismail, crushed by Bugha al-Kabir in 853), later a city-state ruled by its emirs and then a council of elders until David IV of Georgia took it in 1122. The first slice covers central Kartli, the second only the city's district. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Tbilisi'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Lori (Tashir-Dzoraget)
regions.note: Kiurikian (Bagratid) kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget in northern Armenia, nominally a vassal of Ani; the Seljuks took Lori in 1065 and the dynasty survived in Tavush and Matsnaberd until the 12th century (not drawn). Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti
regions.note: Georgian kingdom of Kakheti and Hereti, independent of the united Kingdom of Georgia from c. 1014 until David IV annexed it in 1104. The border data folds it into Georgia; drawn on top. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Syunik
regions.note: Armenian kingdom of Syunik (Kapan), 987–1170. Drawn to 1104, when the Seljuks took Kapan; afterwards it was reduced to a few fortresses (Baghaberd) until 1170. Its frontier on the Aras and with Nakhchivan is approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Syunik'.

regions.name: Kingdom of Vanand (Kars)
regions.note: Bagratid kingdom of Kars (Vanand), founded 963 by Mushegh, brother of Ashot III of Ani; its independence from Ani is uncertain. Ceded to Byzantium by Gagik-Abas in 1065. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Vanand'.

regions.name: Shaddadids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of Dvin and Ganja ruling Arran; drawn at Ganja (Arran between the Kura and the Karabakh hills) until the Seljuk takeover of 1075. A junior branch then governed Ani for the Seljuks and Georgians to 1199 (not drawn, a vassal). Sources: Wikipedia 'Shaddadids'.

regions.name: Sallarid dynasty
regions.note: Daylamite dynasty (Musafirids) that took Azerbaijan in 941 under Marzuban ibn Muhammad; drawn over Azerbaijan until the Rawwadids replaced them in the 980s. Their hold on Arran and Armenia was looser and is not drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sallarid dynasty'.

regions.name: Rawadid dynasty
regions.note: Kurdicised Arab dynasty of Tabriz that ruled Azerbaijan in the late 10th and 11th centuries; Wahsudan submitted to Tughril in 1054 and the Seljuks ended the line in 1071. Sources: Wikipedia 'Rawwadid dynasty'.

regions.name: Hasanwayhids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of the western Jibal (Dinavar, Kermanshah, Hulwan, Shahrizur), recognised by the Buyids; collapsed by 1015 and replaced by the Annazids. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hasanwayhids'.

regions.name: Kakuyids
regions.note: Daylamite dynasty related to the Buyids that ruled Isfahan and Hamadan from c. 1008 (Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar, Avicenna's patron) until Tughril took Isfahan in 1051; afterwards they were Seljuk atabegs of Yazd (to 1141, not drawn). Their brief hold on Rayy is not drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kakuyids'.

regions.name: Marwanids
regions.note: Kurdish dynasty of Diyar Bakr centred on Mayyafariqin (Silvan) and Amid, holding Ahlat and Manzikert for much of the period; ended by the Seljuks in 1085. The border data shows this area as Byzantine; drawn on top. Sources: Wikipedia 'Marwanid dynasty (Diyar Bakr)'.

regions.name: Uqaylid dynasty
regions.note: Arab dynasty of Mosul controlling the Jazira (Nisibis, Sinjar, at times Harran and Raqqa); its height under Muslim ibn Quraysh (1061–1085), who briefly held Aleppo. Mosul passed to the Seljuks in 1096. Extent approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Uqaylid dynasty'.

regions.name: Mirdasid dynasty
regions.note: Arab dynasty of the Banu Kilab ruling the emirate of Aleppo, more or less continuously from Salih ibn Mirdas's capture of the city in 1024 (earlier claims from 1014) until 1080. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mirdasid dynasty'.

regions.name: Mazyadid dynasty (Banu Mazyad)
regions.note: Arab Banu Asad dynasty ruling an autonomous emirate between Kufa and Hit, from c. 961 under the Buyids and then the Seljuks; al-Hilla, founded as their camp, became the capital. Sadaqa I (1086–1108) was the strongest ruler; the emirate ended c. 1150–1160. Extent approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Banu Mazyad'.

regions.name: Burid dynasty (Emirate of Damascus)
regions.note: Turkic dynasty founded by the atabeg Toghtekin, ruling the emirate of Damascus (with the Hauran, Baalbek and at times Homs) nominally under the Seljuks; Nur ad-Din took Damascus in 1154. Extent follows Shepherd's plate 'Asia Minor and the States of the Crusaders in Syria, about 1140' (Emirate of Damascus). Sources: Wikipedia 'Burid dynasty'.

regions.name: Ikhshidid dynasty
regions.note: Turkic governors of Egypt for the Abbasids, in practice autonomous: Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid held Egypt and Palestine from 935 and, after the 944–947 settlement with the Hamdanids, southern Syria with Damascus; the Fatimids took Fustat in 969. The border data shows Egypt as Abbasid; drawn on top. Nominal suzerainty over the Hejaz not drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ikhshidid dynasty'.

regions.name: Ikhshidid dynasty
regions.note: Turkic governors of Egypt for the Abbasids, in practice autonomous: Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid held Egypt and Palestine from 935 and, after the 944–947 settlement with the Hamdanids, southern Syria with Damascus; the Fatimids took Fustat in 969. The border data shows Egypt as Abbasid; drawn on top. Nominal suzerainty over the Hejaz not drawn. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ikhshidid dynasty'.

regions.name: Nizari Ismaili state (Rudbar)
regions.note: The Alamut state founded by Hasan-i Sabbah in 1090: a network of castles rather than a contiguous realm. Drawn: the Rudbar valley of Alamut, Quhistan (from 1091), Girdkuh (from 1096) and the Jabal Bahra castles in Syria (acquired from the 1130s; Masyaf 1140/41). The Mongols took Alamut in 1256; Girdkuh held out to 1270 and the Syrian castles fell to Baybars by 1273 (not drawn after 1256). Sources: Wikipedia 'Nizari Ismaili state'.

regions.name: Salghurids
regions.note: Turkmen atabegs of Fars, vassals first of the Seljuks and then of the Khwarazmshahs and the Mongols, but ruling Fars as a hereditary state until the reign of Abish Khatun, married to an Ilkhanid prince, in the 1280s (Wikidata ends the state in 1282). Extent of Fars approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Salghurids'.

regions.name: Hazaraspids
regions.note: Kurdish (Fadluyid) atabegs of Greater Lur in the Zagros, from the mid-12th century until the Timurids ended them in 1424. Wikipedia dates the dynasty from 1115; 1155 is the usual date for Abu Tahir's atabegate. Extent approximate. Sources: Wikipedia 'Hazaraspids'.

regions.name: Qutlugh-Khanids
regions.note: Khitan dynasty of Kerman founded by Buraq Hajib, vassals of the Mongols; ended 1306/07. Sources: Wikipedia 'Qutlugh-Khanids'.

regions.name: Eldiguzids (Atabegs of Azerbaijan)
regions.note: Atabegs of Azerbaijan, founded by Shams al-Din Eldiguz (atabeg from 1136), who controlled the Seljuk sultans of Iraq and with them Azerbaijan, Arran and the Jibal (first slice, 1146–1194); after Tughril III's death (1194) they held Azerbaijan and Arran until Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah took Tabriz in 1225. The Alamut castles are left outside. Sources: Wikipedia 'Eldiguzids'.

regions.name: Saltukids
regions.note: Turkmen beylik of Erzurum founded after Manzikert (1071); drawn from 1081. Annexed by the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in 1202. Sources: Wikipedia 'Saltukids'.

regions.name: Mengujekids
regions.note: Turkmen beylik of Erzincan, Kemah, Şebinkarahisar and Divriği; the Erzincan line was annexed by Rum in 1228 (the Divriği branch lasted to 1277 as a vassal, not drawn). Sources: Wikipedia 'House of Mengüjek'.

regions.name: Ahlatshahs (Shah-Armens)
regions.note: The Shah-Armens of Ahlat on Lake Van (Bitlis, Van, parts of Muş), 1100–1207; Ahlat passed to the Ayyubids in 1207. Sources: Wikipedia 'Shah-Armens'.

regions.name: Artuqids
regions.note: Turkmen dynasty with branches at Hasankeyf (from 1102; at Amid from 1183), Mardin (from 1106/08) and Harput (1112–1234). Slices: the combined Artuqid lands with Amid left to the Inalids (1102–1183); with Amid (1184–1231); after the Ayyubids took Hasankeyf and Amid (1232) only the Mardin branch, a vassal of the Mongols and Turkmen confederations until the Qara Qoyunlu ended it in 1409. Sources: Wikipedia 'Artuqids'.

regions.name: Eretnids
regions.note: Founded by Eretna, the Ilkhanid governor of Anatolia, who declared himself sultan after the Battle of Karanbük (1343); his realm covered central and eastern Anatolia (Sivas, Kayseri, Amasya, Erzincan, Erzurum). After his death (1352) the east fell away (Erzincan became autonomous) and the state was reduced to the Sivas–Kayseri core; Kadi Burhan al-Din took over in 1381. The border data labels this realm 'Ottoman Empire' (1344–1401); drawn on top. Sources: Wikipedia 'Eretnid dynasty'.

regions.note: Kadi Burhan al-Din, the Eretnid vizier, took over the Eretnid lands in 1381 and ruled them as sultan from Sivas until he was killed by the Aq Qoyunlu c. 1398; Bayezid I then annexed Sivas. Sources: Wikipedia 'Kadi Burhan al-Din'.

regions.name: Beylik of Erzincan (Emirate of Erzincan)
regions.note: Emirate centred on Erzincan, autonomous after Eretna's death (1352) under Ahi Ayna and his successors; Mutahharten (1379–1403) was a vassal of Timur. Annexed by the Qara Qoyunlu c. 1410. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Erzincan'.

regions.name: Beylik of Tacettin
regions.note: Small Turkmen principality of Niksar and the coast at Ünye and Çarşamba (the Byzantine Limnia), 1348–1428, wedged between Trebizond, the Eretnids and the Ottomans. Sources: Wikipedia 'Emirate of Limnia'.

regions.name: Beylik of Lâdik (İnançoğulları)
regions.note: The İnançoğulları beylik of Lâdik (Denizli), from the Seljuk collapse of the 1260s; later dependent on the Germiyanids and absorbed c. 1368. The border data shows the area as Hamid and Germiyan territory; drawn on top. Dates from Wikidata (Q717451). Sources: Wikipedia 'Beylik of Lâdik'.

regions.name: Beylik of Alaiye
regions.note: Alanya (Alaiye) and its hinterland, semi-autonomous after the Seljuk defeat at Köse Dağ (1243) and a beylik from c. 1293, at times under the Karamanids or Lusignan Cyprus; briefly passed to the Mamluks in the 1420s and was taken by the Ottomans in 1471. Sources: Wikipedia 'Alaiye'.

regions.name: Mamluk dynasty of Iraq
regions.note: The Georgian mamluk pashas of Baghdad, from Hasan Pasha (1704) and his son Ahmad to Dawud Pasha, governed Baghdad and Basra (with Shahrizor at times) with near-complete autonomy from the Ottoman sultan until the Ottoman reconquest of 1831. title: Princely states of India
summary: When the British Crown took over from the East India Company in 1858, it did not rule all of India directly. About two-fifths of the subcontinent stayed under Indian princes: maharajas, nawabs, the Nizam of Hyderabad and hundreds of minor chiefs. Many of their states had signed 'subsidiary alliances' with the Company, giving up control of foreign affairs and accepting British troops in return for protection. After 1858 the Crown inherited these treaties and claimed 'paramountcy': the rulers ran their own internal affairs, but Britain controlled their defence and foreign relations, kept a Resident or Political Agent at their courts, and could depose a ruler for misrule. In 1947 there were 565 recognised states, from Hyderabad and Kashmir, each larger than many European countries, to estates of a few villages. When British rule ended, paramountcy lapsed and each ruler was asked to join India or Pakistan. Most signed Instruments of Accession by 15 August 1947. Junagadh's Nawab chose Pakistan, but India took over in November 1947; Kashmir's Maharaja acceded to India in October 1947 during a tribal invasion; Kalat joined Pakistan in March 1948; and Hyderabad was taken over by the Indian Army in September 1948. These outlines are traced from the Imperial Gazetteer of India maps of 1909 and from OpenHistoricalMap. The largest states are drawn singly; the hundreds of small ones are grouped by agency. Boundaries are approximate, and they show the states as they were around 1909.

regions.name: Hyderabad
regions.note: The Nizam's state in the Deccan, one of the two largest princely states with Jammu and Kashmir. The Nizam did not accede in 1947; the Indian Army took control between 13 and 18 September 1948 (Operation Polo). Outline from OpenHistoricalMap, matching the 1909 Imperial Gazetteer map; Berar is shown separately. Drawn area c. 213,900 km².

regions.name: Berar (Hyderabad Assigned Districts)
regions.note: Assigned by the Nizam to East India Company administration under an 1853 treaty, so it was Hyderabad's territory but British-run. Leased permanently to the British on 5 November 1902 and joined to the Central Provinces from 1 October 1903. Drawn area c. 43,600 km².

regions.name: Mysore (under British commission)
regions.capital: Mysore (Bangalore was the seat of the British commission 1831–1881)
regions.note: The British took over direct administration of Mysore in 1831. The state kept its identity and was handed back (the 'rendition') in 1881 to Chamarajendra Wadiyar X. Drawn area c. 79,600 km².

regions.name: Mysore
regions.note: Ruled again by the Wodeyar dynasty after the 1881 rendition; one of the largest states in the south. Joined the Indian Union on 9 August 1947. Drawn area c. 79,600 km².

regions.name: Jammu and Kashmir
regions.note: Ruled by the Dogra maharajas, including Ladakh and the Gilgit region (the outline follows OpenHistoricalMap and includes claimed frontier areas). Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India dated 26 October 1947; Mountbatten accepted it on 27 October. Drawn area c. 186,200 km².

regions.name: Cochin
regions.note: Small kingdom north of Travancore, around Ernakulam and Trichur. It acceded to India in 1947 and merged with Travancore on 1 July 1949. Its boundary with Travancore is approximate (traced from the 1909 Madras map). Drawn area c. 3,100 km².

regions.name: Travancore
regions.note: Southern kingdom on the Malabar coast. Its ruler agreed to accede to India on 12 August 1947; it merged with Cochin on 1 July 1949. Outline from OpenHistoricalMap, with the Cochin part cut off along the 1909 map's boundary (approximate). Drawn area c. 20,000 km².

regions.name: Cutch
regions.note: Peninsula state ruled by the Rao; the outline includes the Great Rann. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 42,200 km².

regions.name: Kolhapur
regions.note: Maratha state of the Bhonsle line of Shivaji, the chief state of the Kolhapur and Southern Maratha Country agency. Outline from OpenHistoricalMap. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 7,700 km².

regions.name: Sikkim
regions.note: Himalayan kingdom, a British protectorate from the 1861 Treaty of Tumlong. It did not join India in 1947; it became an Indian protectorate in 1950 and an Indian state in 1975. Drawn area c. 7,100 km².

regions.name: Manipur
regions.note: Hill kingdom on the Burma frontier. Acceded to India on 11 August 1947. Drawn area c. 22,400 km².

regions.name: Hill Tippera (Tripura)
regions.note: Kingdom east of Bengal, called Hill Tippera in British records. Acceded to India on 13 August 1947. Drawn area c. 10,500 km².

regions.name: Bahawalpur
regions.note: Muslim-ruled state on the Sutlej, south-west of the Punjab. The Nawab signed accession to Pakistan on 5 October 1947, accepted on 9 October; the first state to accede to Pakistan. Drawn area c. 45,000 km².

regions.name: Khairpur
regions.note: State of the Talpur Mirs in Sind. Acceded to Pakistan on 3 October 1947. Drawn area c. 16,200 km².

regions.name: Kalat (with Kharan, Las Bela and Makran)
regions.note: The Khan of Kalat headed a confederacy of Baloch chiefs; Kharan, Las Bela and Makran are included in this outline (Kharan was separated from Kalat as its own state in the 1930s). Kharan, Las Bela and Makran acceded to Pakistan first; Kalat acceded on 27 March 1948. Kalat, Kharan and Las Bela outlines are from OpenHistoricalMap; Makran is traced from the 1909 map. Drawn area c. 191,500 km².

regions.name: Chitral
regions.note: Mountain state of the Mehtar, allied with the British from 1885 (agreement of 1891). The Mehtar signed the Instrument of Accession to Pakistan on 6 November 1947. The outline is hand-drawn from the 1909 North-West Frontier Province map and is larger than the 14,860 km² given for 1951. Drawn area c. 19,000 km².

regions.name: Bikaner
regions.note: Rathore state in the Thar Desert, in the Rajputana Agency. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 59,100 km².

regions.name: Jaisalmer
regions.note: Bhati Rajput desert state in the Rajputana Agency. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 40,000 km².

regions.name: Jodhpur (Marwar)
regions.note: The largest state in Rajputana, ruled by Rathores. Acceded to India in August 1947. Drawn area c. 92,400 km².

regions.name: Jaipur
regions.note: Kachhwaha state, including the Shekhawati chiefships. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 34,400 km².

regions.name: Udaipur (Mewar)
regions.note: Senior Rajput house (Sisodias) in the Aravalli hills. The small state of Shahpura sits inside this outline. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 32,600 km².

regions.name: Kotah (with Jhalawar)
regions.note: Kotah and Jhalawar (carved out of Kotah) formed the Kotah and Jhalawar Agency; they are drawn together because their boundary cannot be read reliably on the 1909 map. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 17,500 km².

regions.name: Gwalior
regions.note: Maratha state of the Scindias. This outline is the main northern block (Gwalior, Bhind, Sheopur, Narwar, Isagarh); Gwalior's Malwa districts (Ujjain, Mandsaur, Shajapur and others) are interleaved with other states and are inside the Central India group. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 33,600 km².

regions.name: Indore
regions.note: Maratha state of the Holkars. Outline is the main Indore–Nimar block; detached parts (such as Rampura-Bhanpura) are inside the Central India group. Its edges are approximate. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 12,500 km².

regions.name: Bhopal
regions.note: Muslim-ruled state, for much of the 19th century governed by begums. Its edges are approximate. Shown until 1947 with the other Central India states. Drawn area c. 14,800 km².

regions.name: Rewa
regions.note: The largest state in Baghelkhand. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 34,400 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Amreli)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 2,800 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Okhamandal)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 600 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Kodinar)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 500 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Amreli)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 300 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Kadi division)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 8,600 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Baroda division)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 4,100 km².

regions.name: Baroda (Navsari division)
regions.note: A detached division of Baroda, the Gaekwad's Maratha state, whose territory lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 3,100 km².

regions.name: Junagadh
regions.note: Muslim-ruled state on the Kathiawar peninsula. The Nawab acceded to Pakistan, fled on 26 October 1947, and on 7 November 1947 the state's council invited India to take over; a February 1948 plebiscite favoured India. Edges approximate. Drawn area c. 7,400 km².

regions.name: Bastar
regions.note: The largest of the Chhattisgarh feudatory states, a forested plateau. Merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948 after acceding in 1947. Drawn area c. 32,200 km².

regions.name: Surguja
regions.note: Hill state of the Chota Nagpur plateau, among the Central Provinces feudatories in 1909. Merged on 1 January 1948. Drawn area c. 13,300 km².

regions.name: Mayurbhanj
regions.note: The largest of the Orissa feudatory states. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 9,200 km².

regions.name: Patiala
regions.note: The leading Sikh (Phulkian) state. The outline is its main block; the small states of Nabha and Malerkotla, which lie in pockets within it, are not separated. Patiala's Narnaul district lies far to the south (not shown separately). Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 15,000 km².

regions.name: Tehri Garhwal
regions.note: Hill state in the Himalaya north of Dehra Dun, under the United Provinces. Traced from the small-scale 1909 empire map only, so its outline is coarse. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 9,500 km².

regions.name: Pudukkottai

regions.name: Rajputana Agency (other states): Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Karauli, Bundi, Tonk

regions.name: Rajputana Agency (other states): Sirohi

regions.name: Rajputana Agency (other states): Kishangarh

regions.name: Central India Agency (other states): Charkhari

The many small states and interlocking enclaves cannot be drawn singly from the 1909 map. All acceded in 1947–48. Drawn area c. 500 km².

regions.name: Central India Agency (other states): small Bundelkhand states near Baoni

regions.name: Kathiawar states
regions.note: The many states of the Kathiawar peninsula (among them Nawanagar, Bhavnagar, Porbandar, Gondal, Morvi and Dhrangadhra). Grouped because they cannot be drawn singly. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 43,400 km².

regions.name: Gujarat states: Palanpur, Radhanpur, Idar, Rajpipla, Lunavada, Chhota Udaipur
regions.note: States of the Palanpur, Mahi Kantha and Rewa Kantha agencies and other Gujarat states under the Bombay government. Grouped because they cannot be drawn singly. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 36,700 km².

regions.name: Gujarat states: tract near Cambay
regions.note: States of the Palanpur, Mahi Kantha and Rewa Kantha agencies and other Gujarat states under the Bombay government. Grouped because they cannot be drawn singly. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 1,400 km².

regions.name: Gujarat states: Dharampur and Bansda
regions.note: States of the Palanpur, Mahi Kantha and Rewa Kantha agencies and other Gujarat states under the Bombay government. Grouped because they cannot be drawn singly. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 1,100 km².

regions.note: The Southern Maratha Country states and Satara jagirs (Sangli, Miraj, Jamkhandi, Mudhol, Bhor, Aundh, Phaltan, Akalkot and others) and Savantvadi, under the Bombay government. Grouped. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 600 km².

regions.note: The Southern Maratha Country states and Satara jagirs (Sangli, Miraj, Jamkhandi, Mudhol, Bhor, Aundh, Phaltan, Akalkot and others) and Savantvadi, under the Bombay government. Grouped. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 400 km².

regions.name: Chhattisgarh feudatory states: Kawardha
regions.note: Feudatory states of the Central Provinces (later the Chhattisgarh States Agency). Merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948. Drawn area c. 3,000 km².

regions.name: Orissa feudatory states: Patna, Kalahandi, Sonpur, Bamra, Gangpur, Keonjhar, Dhenkanal, Bonai, Nayagarh, Baud, Talcher, Nilgiri, Athmallik
regions.note: The Orissa Tributary States; with the Chhattisgarh states they were later grouped in the Eastern States Agency. Merger agreements of December 1947 took effect on 1 January 1948. Drawn area c. 60,000 km².

regions.name: Saraikela and Kharsawan (Chota Nagpur states)
regions.note: Two small Chota Nagpur states under Bengal in 1909; later in the Eastern States Agency. Merged on 1 January 1948. Drawn area c. 1,500 km².

regions.note: Hill states under the Punjab government (Chamba, Mandi, Suket, Bilaspur, Sirmur, Bashahr and the Simla Hill States). Grouped. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 7,000 km².

title: South Asian kingdoms to 1000 CE
summary: Kingdoms of South Asia before 1000 CE that the base border data leaves out: the Western Gangas of Karnataka, the Licchavis of Nepal, Zhangzhung in Western Tibet, the Hindu Shahis, the kingdoms of Sindh and Multan, the Vishnukundinas and Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra, the Kalachuris, the Chera Perumals, the dynasties of Odisha and Dakshina Kosala, the Later Guptas, the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri and Porus. Extents are approximate reconstructions from regional descriptions in the sources, trimmed to stay clear of the states the atlas already draws.

regions.name: Western Ganga kingdom (Gangavadi)
regions.capital: Kolar (Kuvalala), then Talakad (Talakadu) on the Kaveri from c. 390
regions.note: Gangavadi: the modern Mysore, Hassan, Mandya, Ramanagara, Chamarajanagar, Tumkur, Kolar and Bangalore districts (Wikipedia). Before c. 470 only the eastern districts round Kolar and Talakad are drawn; Sendraka (Chikkamagaluru, Belur), Punnata and the northern Kongu country were added by c. 470, and Kongu was held, contested with the Pandyas, into the 9th century. The Gangas were feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas (6th–8th c.) and, after a century of resistance, allies of the Rashtrakutas; they are drawn as their own kingdom throughout. The Tungabhadra lands granted after Takkolam (949) are not drawn. Ended when the Cholas took Gangavadi c. 1000. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

regions.name: Licchavi kingdom of Nepal
regions.note: The kingdom centred on the Kathmandu Valley; settlement reached east towards Banepa, west towards Tistung and north-west towards Gorkha (Wikipedia: Licchavi (kingdom)). The outer limits in the hills are a convention. Dates c. 400–879; the dynasty was followed by the Thakuris. Tibet claimed overlordship in the mid-7th century. title: South Asian kingdoms, 1550–1857
summary: From the fall of Vijayanagara's capital to the Revolt of 1857, the map's border data (Cliopatria) draws the Mughal, Maratha, Durrani and British realms and a few successor states, but leaves out many kingdoms that ruled themselves. This layer adds them. In the south: Travancore, Cochin, the Zamorin's Calicut, the Keladi Nayakas, the last Aravidu kings of Vijayanagara, the Nayaks of Gingee, and Mysore redrawn through the Wodeyar, Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan periods. In the Deccan and centre: the Gond kingdoms of Garha-Mandla, Deogarh and Chanda, Bastar, Ratanpur, Hyderabad after 1799, Nagpur, Satara, and the Holkar, Scindia and Gaekwad states after 1818. In the north and west: Rajputana after the Mughal collapse, state by state (Mewar, Marwar, Amber with its Shekhawati tributaries, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Kota, Bundi, Jhalawar, Kishangarh, Sirohi, Dungarpur, Banswara, Partabgarh, Karauli, Jat Bharatpur and Dholpur, Alwar, Tonk, and Maratha- and then British-held Ajmer), Bahawalpur, Rohilkhand, the reduced Awadh of 1803–56, Kumaon, Garhwal, Ladakh and Sikkim. In the east: the Ahom, Koch, Kachari, Jaintia, Manipur and Tripura kingdoms. Also Kutch and the Khanate of Kalat. Outlines are traced from the Imperial Gazetteer Atlas historical plates (1765, 1805, 1837, 1857), the Rajputana states from its 1909 Rajputana plate, where those show a state, and otherwise reconstructed from rivers, hill lines and the later princely-state borders; they are approximate. States that continued as princely states end in 1857, where the princely-states layer begins.

regions.name: Venad (early Travancore)
regions.note: Venad, the kingdom from which Travancore grew, held the south-western tip of India: Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari, with Attingal. Kollam (Desinganad), Kayamkulam and the lands further north were separate chiefdoms. Its 16th–17th century rulers are poorly documented; the outline follows the Wikipedia description of Venad's core districts, and the northern edge near Varkala is a convention. Sibling layers may draw Venad before 1550.

regions.name: Travancore under Marthanda Varma
regions.note: Marthanda Varma (r. 1729–1758) turned Venad into Travancore: he annexed Attingal, Kollam/Desinganad (1742) and Kayamkulam (1746) and beat the Dutch at Colachel (1741). One outline is drawn for this whole phase of conquest, with its northern edge just beyond Kayamkulam, so the 1730s are drawn somewhat too large.

regions.name: Kingdom of Travancore
regions.note: After taking Ambalappuzha, Thekkumkur and Vadakkumkur (1749–54; Treaty of Mavelikkara with Cochin, 1753), Travancore reached roughly the extent it kept until 1949. Plates 28 and 29 of the Imperial Gazetteer Atlas show it this way in 1765, 1805, 1837 and 1857. It accepted a subsidiary alliance with the East India Company (1795, 1805). Drawn here to 1857; the princely-states layer takes over in 1858. The border with Cochin around Kochi was a patchwork of enclaves and is simplified here.

regions.name: Kingdom of Cochin
regions.note: Cochin was a Portuguese ally (1503–1663) and then a Dutch protectorate (1663–1795). The Zamorin occupied its northern districts in 1756–62, Mysore exacted tribute from 1774, and it became a British subsidiary state in 1791/1809. The outline follows the Cochin State of plates 28–29 (1805–1857), which matches the 1909 state. Its 16th–17th-century borders with the Zamorin and with the Travancore chiefdoms moved often and are not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Calicut (the Zamorin)

rulers.name: Manavikraman (various Zamorins of the same title)
Zamorin allied with the Dutch against the Portuguese
Zamorin who burned his palace as Hyder Ali arrived

regions.note: The Zamorins held south Malabar, from the Korapuzha river south to Chettuva, inland through Ernad and Nilambur, and fought Portugal and Cochin for a century. Palakkad (Palghat) under its own raja, and the northern Kolathiri lands, are outside the outline. Hyder Ali conquered Calicut in 1766. Zamorins took personal names that are rarely recorded, so the rulers listed are by event. The inland edge is approximate.

regions.name: Keladi Nayakas (Ikkeri / Bednur)
regions.note: The Keladi Nayakas were Vijayanagara governors who became independent after Talikota (1565). They held Shimoga and Chikmagalur on the plateau and the Canara coast from about Kasaragod to Honnavar. Shivappa Nayaka drove the Portuguese from the Canara ports. Hyder Ali took Bidanur in 1763. The northern edge (Sonda, Banavasi) and the line against Mysore and Coorg are approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (Wodeyar principality)
regions.note: This is the small Wodeyar principality around Mysore while it was a Vijayanagara feudatory. Raja Wodeyar took Srirangapatna from the Vijayanagara viceroy in 1610. In this period the layer replaces the map's Cliopatria 'Kingdom of Mysore' polygons with its own outlines (1572–1857).

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (Srirangapatna)
regions.note: After taking Srirangapatna in 1610, the Wodeyars expanded over Mandya, southern Hassan, Chamarajanagar and the Kaveri country under Raja Wodeyar and Kanthirava Narasaraja I. The edges are approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore under Chikka Devaraja and successors
regions.note: Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (r. 1673–1704) brought Mysore close to its later core: Hassan, Tumkur and Bangalore (bought from the Mughals in 1689), with Baramahal and Salem on the eastern edge. The outline follows the Cliopatria extent for 1673–1798 with Coorg and Keladi left out. From 1734 the Dalavayi brothers, and from 1761 Hyder Ali, held real power.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Bednur)
regions.note: Hyder Ali took Bidanur (the Keladi kingdom) and the Canara coast in 1763 and Sonda in 1764. Sira was also taken in the 1760s, but its exact extent is not drawn.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Malabar)
regions.note: Hyder conquered Malabar in 1766 (Calicut, the Kolathiri lands, Palakkad), Coorg in 1773, and held Coimbatore, Dindigul and Baramahal. Cochin paid tribute but is drawn separately; Travancore stayed independent. Chitradurga (taken 1779) lies outside this outline.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
regions.note: The kingdom was at its largest after Hyder took Bellary and Gooty (1775–76) and Chitradurga, Cuddapah and the Savanur country (1776–79). The Treaty of Gajendragad (1787) returned some northern districts to the Marathas. The northern edge is a mainstream simplification along the Tungabhadra and Krishna watershed. Plate 28 (1765) and contemporary accounts were used to check it.

regions.name: Mysore under Tipu Sultan after the Treaty of Seringapatam
regions.note: The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) took half of Tipu's lands. Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul and Salem–Baramahal went to the Company, and the lands north of the Tungabhadra to the Nizam and the Marathas. Tipu kept the plateau, Coimbatore and Canara. He died when Srirangapatna fell on 4 May 1799. Whether Wayanad stayed with Mysore is disputed; it is left out here.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (restored Wodeyars)
regions.note: In 1799 the Company restored the Wodeyars to a reduced, landlocked Mysore that matches the princely state of plate 29 (1837, 1857) and of 1909. The Company ran it directly through a commission from 1831 to 1881. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Penukonda and Chandragiri)
regions.note: After Talikota (1565) and the sack of Hampi, the Aravidu kings ruled from Penukonda and then Chandragiri. They still held Anantapur, Chittoor, Kolar and the Vellore country and claimed overlordship of the Nayaks of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee and of Mysore. The map's Cliopatria 'Vijayanagara Empire' stops in 1571, so these last decades were blank. Only lands under direct Aravidu rule are drawn. Their northern and eastern edges against Golconda and Bijapur moved often and are approximate.

regions.name: Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Chandragiri and Vellore)
regions.note: The civil war after Venkatapati Raya's death (Battle of Toppur, 1616), followed by Golconda's and Bijapur's advance into the Carnatic, reduced the empire to the Chandragiri–Vellore country. Vellore fell around 1646, which is taken as the empire's end (Wikipedia: 1336–1646); Sriranga III lived on in exile until 1678. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Nayaks of Gingee
regions.note: Gingee was one of the three Tamil Nayakships under Vijayanagara, alongside Madurai and Thanjavur (both drawn on the map). It held the land between the Palar and the Kollidam (Coleroon) until Bijapur took the fort in 1649. It is drawn from 1572 only, because the map draws it inside the Vijayanagara Empire before then. Its line with the Aravidu territory to the north and with Thanjavur to the south is approximate.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (the Nizam's dominions)
regions.note: The map's Cliopatria Hyderabad stops in 1798. The Nizam entered a subsidiary alliance in 1798 and in 1800 ceded his share of the Mysore conquests (the 'Ceded Districts': Bellary, Cuddapah and others). From then on the state matched the Nizam's dominions of plate 28 (1805), plate 29 (1837, 1857) and 1909. Berar was then still under the Bhonsles of Nagpur.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (with Berar)
regions.note: The Treaty of Deogaon (1803) gave the Nizam Berar west of the Wardha river, which is drawn as part of Hyderabad. Plate 29 (1837) colours Berar with the Nizam's lands. In 1853 Berar was 'assigned' to the Company to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (Berar assigned)
regions.note: After the Treaty of 1853 assigned Berar to the Company, plate 29 (1857) still shades it with the Nizam's lands (formal sovereignty stayed with the Nizam). Here it is left out, because the Company administered it. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Nagpur (Bhonsle)
regions.note: After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (Sitabuldi, 1817) the Bhonsles lost the Saugor and Narmada territories and kept Nagpur, Wardha (east of the river), Chanda, Bhandara, Chhindwara and Chhattisgarh as a protected state. The Company annexed it by lapse in 1853. Plate 29 (1837, 'Bhonsla') shows this extent. Before 1818 the Bhonsle lands are part of the map's Maratha Empire. Bastar and the other feudatory chiefdoms are left out.

regions.name: Satara State (Bhonsle rump)
regions.note: After the Peshwa's fall the Company set up Shivaji's descendant Pratap Singh in a small state around Satara. It was annexed by lapse in 1848–49. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Indore State (Holkar)
regions.note: After Mahidpur (1817) and the Treaty of Mandsaur (1818), Holkar's state was reduced to scattered districts under British protection. Drawn here are its Indore–Nimar core and (as a separate region) the Rampura–Bhanpura district; smaller enclaves are left out. Before 1818 Holkar's lands are part of the map's Maratha Empire.

regions.name: Indore State (Rampura–Bhanpura)
regions.note: This is Holkar's northern district around Rampura and Bhanpura, between Mewar, Kota and Scindia's Malwa lands. The edges are approximate. Trimmed where the Rajputana states drawn in this layer (Dholpur, Karauli, Kota, Tonk's districts, Partabgarh) lie.

regions.name: Gwalior State (Scindia)
regions.note: The map draws Scindia's state from 1820 to 1845 (as a relabelled Cliopatria polygon), but nothing from 1846. This outline continues the northern block of that polygon (Gwalior, Narwar, Guna, Bhind) to 1857. It is unchanged by the Gwalior campaign of 1843 (Maharajpur, Panniar), which brought a British-officered contingent but little loss of land. Trimmed where the Rajputana states drawn in this layer (Dholpur, Karauli, Kota, Tonk's districts, Partabgarh) lie.

regions.name: Gwalior State (Scindia's Malwa districts)
regions.note: Scindia's Malwa districts around Ujjain, Shajapur and Mandsaur, drawn approximately without Holkar's and the small Rajput states' enclaves. Trimmed where the Rajputana states drawn in this layer (Dholpur, Karauli, Kota, Tonk's districts, Partabgarh) lie.

regions.name: Baroda State (Gaekwad; Baroda district)
regions.note: From 1802 the Gaekwads were allied with the Company, and after 1818 their state, scattered across Gujarat, was a protected state. Only the two largest blocks are drawn: the Baroda district here and the Kadi district separately. Navsari and Amreli are left out. Before 1818 Gujarat is drawn inside the map's Maratha Empire.

regions.name: Baroda State (Gaekwad; Kadi district)
regions.note: The Gaekwads' northern district around Kadi and Patan. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Cutch (Kingdom of Kutch)
regions.note: The Jadeja Raos ruled Kutch and the Rann from Bhuj, founded in 1549. They paid tribute to the Mughals from the 1590s while ruling themselves, and came under British protection in 1819. The map draws Kutch inside the Mughal Empire (to 1751) and then leaves it blank, so it is drawn here as its own kingdom throughout. Plates 28 and 29 show 'Cutch' with this extent. The northern edge across the Rann is a convention. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Udaipur)
regions.note: Mewar was the one major Rajput kingdom that refused Mughal suzerainty. Akbar took Chittor in 1568, and Pratap fought at Haldighati (1576) and later won back most of the hill country; Amar Singh I submitted by treaty in 1615. The map draws Mewar inside the Mughal Empire from 1564, so this region overlaps that outline. The extent is its 1909 territory, with Chittor (lost 1568) included throughout; this is approximate.

regions.name: Bahawalpur State
regions.note: The Daudpotra nawabs, who came from Shikarpur in Sindh, founded Bahawalpur on the left bank of the Sutlej in 1748 and ruled the river strip and the desert behind it. They acknowledged the Durrani kings in name; the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar kept Ranjit Singh to the right bank of the Sutlej, and in 1833 the Nawab made a subsidiary alliance with the British. The map's Mughal (to 1751), Durrani (to 1827) and Sikh (1820–48) outlines reach over this land; the Sikh one is cut back (see the corrections), the others are drawn underneath. The extent is the 1909 state (with Sabzalkot and Bhung, granted in 1849), so it is approximate for the 18th century. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar (Jodhpur)

Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards. Ajmer (Maratha-held, then British) and Kishangarh are drawn as their own regions.

regions.name: Shekhawati (Shekhawat chiefs under Amber)
regions.capital: Jhunjhunu, Sikar, Khetri and other chiefs' seats
regions.note: The Shekhawat Rajput chiefs of Sikar, Khetri, Jhunjhunu, Nawalgarh and the other thikanas north of Jaipur ruled their estates themselves but were tributaries of Amber (Jaipur), so the region shares Amber's colour. The name was in use by 1803. Its southern edge (south of Danta, Shrimadhopur and Neem-ka-Thana) is not printed on Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931) and follows the later Sikar and Jhunjhunu districts; it is approximate. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer includes it in Jaipur from 1858.

regions.name: Alwar State

rulers.name: Bakhtawar Singh
rulers.when: treaty with the East India Company, 1803

regions.note: The Naruka Kachhwahas of Macheri, a branch of the Amber house, built Rajgarh with Jaipur's leave; when Bharatpur defaulted on the Alwar fort garrison's pay, Pratap Singh took the fort, renounced his allegiance to Jaipur and established Alwar State in 1775. In 1803 Alwar became the first Rajputana state in permanent alliance with the East India Company. The outline is traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931). The map's Mughal and Maratha outlines over it are cut back (see the corrections). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Bharatpur (Jat kingdom)
regions.note: The Jat state of the Sinsinwars. Under Suraj Mal (1755–63) its power stretched far beyond this outline, over Agra (held 1761–74), Mathura and Mewat; that larger dominion is not drawn. The outline is the later state, traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931), which withstood Lake's siege in 1805 and fell to Combermere in 1826. The map's Mughal outline over it is cut back for 1752–1803. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Dholpur State
regions.note: Rana Kirat Singh, the Jat ruler of Gohad, gave Gohad up to the British (who returned it to the Scindias) and was given Dholpur, Bari and Rajakhera instead, founding Dholpur State in 1805; it came under British protection in 1818. Before 1805 the map's Maratha (Scindia) outline covers this land. The outline is traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Karauli State
regions.note: The Jadon Rajputs ruled Karauli, in the ravines south of the Chambal's bend, from the 14th century. They paid tribute to the Marathas in the later 18th century (the map's Maratha outline covers Karauli then) and signed a treaty with the East India Company on 9 November 1817. The outline, inside Karauli's yellow border band on Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931), leaves Hindaun and Gangapur to Jaipur. Rulers' reign dates were not checked for this layer. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Tonk (Holkar's pargana)
regions.note: Madho Singh I of Jaipur gave Holkar the parganas of Rampura, Bhanpura and Tonk for his help in winning the Jaipur throne (1753 in Wikipedia's Madho Singh article, 1757 in its Malhar Rao Holkar article). Holkar was one of the Maratha confederacy's great chiefs; the map's Maratha outline does not reach this district, so it is drawn on its own. The outline is the Tonk pargana as traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931).

regions.name: Rampura–Aligarh (Holkar's)
regions.note: The Rampura (later Aligarh) district east of Tonk was given to Amir Khan by the British in 1817. Before that it is assumed to have followed Tonk in Holkar's hands; this is uncertain. Outline traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931).

regions.name: Tonk State
regions.note: Amir Khan, a Pashtun commander in Yashwant Rao Holkar's service, received Tonk from Holkar in 1806; after the Third Anglo-Maratha War he submitted to the East India Company, which recognised him in 1817 as Nawab of a state of six separate districts: Tonk, Aligarh (Rampura) and Nimbahera in Rajputana, and Chhabra, Pirawa and Sironj in Central India. The Rajputana districts are traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931); Chhabra and Sironj follow the 1909 princely-state outlines and Pirawa is placed from the plate (approximate). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Jhalawar State
regions.note: Zalim Singh Jhala ruled Kota as regent for more than forty years. In 1838, with Kota's grudging consent, the British created a principality for his descendants from districts worth a third of Kota's revenue, and his grandson Madan Singh became its first Maharaj Rana. The outline is the 1909 state (Patan, Pachpahar, Dag and Gangdhar) traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931); the 1838 grant may have differed, so it is approximate. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kishangarh State
regions.note: A Rathore state founded in 1611 by Kishan Singh, a Jodhpur prince in Mughal service. It came under British protection on 26 March 1818. A rival line ruled from Rupnagar in 1756–81 (not drawn separately). The outline follows the 1909 princely-state outline. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Sirohi State
regions.note: The Deora Chauhan state round Mount Abu. In the early 19th century it suffered from wars with Jodhpur, which claimed suzerainty; it sought British protection in 1817, Jodhpur's claim was disallowed, and a treaty followed in 1823. The outline follows the 1909 princely-state outline. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Dungarpur State
regions.note: The elder Sisodia line of Vagad, west of the Mahi. Under Maratha control from the 1730s, it came under British protection by treaty in 1818. The Mahi border with Banswara is traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Banswara State
regions.note: Split from Dungarpur after 1527, east of the Mahi. By the end of the 18th century it paid tribute to the Maratha Raja of Dhar; the Maharawal asked for British protection in 1812 and made a subsidiary alliance in 1818. Outline traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Partabgarh State (Pratapgarh)
regions.note: A Sisodia offshoot of Mewar (Kanthal), ruled from Deolia and, from 1698, from Pratapgarh. A treaty with the British in 1804 was cancelled by Cornwallis; a new one in 1818 made it a protected state. Outline traced from Imperial Gazetteer Atlas of India plate 36 (Rajputana with Ajmer-Merwara, 1909/1931). Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Ajmer (held by the Scindias)

rulers.name: Daulat Rao Scindia
rulers.when: ceded Ajmer to the British, 25 June 1818

regions.note: Wikipedia's Ajmer article dates the Scindia conquest of Ajmer to 1752; Daulat Rao Scindia ceded the district to the British by the treaty of 25 June 1818. Scindia was one of the Maratha confederacy's great chiefs; the map's Maratha outline does not reach Ajmer, so it is drawn on its own. The outline is the gap the 1909 states leave, with the small Kekri tract to the south-east; it is approximate.
