regions.name: Sintashta culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: A Bronze Age culture of the steppe east of the southern Urals, in Russia and northern Kazakhstan. Its people lived in fortified settlements such as Sintashta and Arkaim, worked copper on a large scale, and buried their leaders with horses, weapons and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots. Many scholars see it as the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Andronovo culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: A family of related Late Bronze Age cultures of herders and farmers across the Kazakh steppe, from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei and south to the edges of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. They kept cattle, horses, sheep, goats and camels, farmed where they could, and worked copper and bronze. Scholars widely link them with early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Ochre Coloured Pottery culture (with the Copper Hoards)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: A Bronze Age culture of the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, eastern Punjab, Haryana and north-eastern Rajasthan, named after its orange-red pottery that rubs off on the fingers. It overlaps with the Late Harappans and is linked to hoards of copper weapons and tools. The cemetery of Sinauli, with its wheeled carts, belongs to it. It was followed by the Painted Grey Ware culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Late Harappan (Cemetery H, Jhukar and Rangpur phases)
regions.evidenceNote: No readable writing; known from excavated villages and cemeteries and from radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The phase after the great Indus cities declined, when settlement shifted east towards Haryana and the Ganga-Yamuna doab and south into Gujarat. Regional cultures replaced the shared urban style: Cemetery H in Punjab and Haryana, known for its painted burial jars, Jhukar in Sindh and Rangpur in Gujarat. Writing and seals faded, and people lived in smaller farming villages.
regions.note: No readable writing; known from excavated villages and cemeteries and from radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Late Harappan (Cemetery H, Jhukar and Rangpur phases)
regions.evidenceNote: No readable writing; known from excavated villages and cemeteries and from radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The phase after the great Indus cities declined, when settlement shifted east towards Haryana and the Ganga-Yamuna doab and south into Gujarat. Regional cultures replaced the shared urban style: Cemetery H in Punjab and Haryana, known for its painted burial jars, Jhukar in Sindh and Rangpur in Gujarat. Writing and seals faded, and people lived in smaller farming villages.
regions.note: No readable writing; known from excavated villages and cemeteries and from radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Malwa culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1600–1300 BCE (calibrated dates suggest a start as early as 2000–1750 BCE)
regions.summary: A Chalcolithic farming culture of the Malwa plateau in Madhya Pradesh and parts of northern Maharashtra, known from sites such as Navdatoli and Kayatha. Its people grew wheat, barley, pulses and later rice, kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, and painted their pottery in black on red. Most villages were unplanned clusters of houses, though the largest had walls.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Yaz culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The early Iron Age culture of Margiana, Bactria and Sogdia, which followed the BMAC. Its people lived in rural settlements around fortified mudbrick platforms and citadels, dug irrigation canals, and used hand-made and later wheel-made pottery with iron sickles and arrowheads. Burials almost disappear in this period, and many scholars link it to the early Iranian world of the Avesta.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Jorwe culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: A Chalcolithic culture of the Deccan in Maharashtra, named after the village of Jorwe. Over 200 settlements are known, from farming villages to herders' camps; the largest, Daimabad, had a mud wall. Its people grew barley, wheat, millets and pulses, and made red pottery painted in black. Its villages suggest chiefdoms rather than states.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Gandhara grave culture (Swat protohistoric graves)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1400–800 BCE in Swat (Italian mission); some scholars extend it to the historic period
regions.summary: A protohistoric culture of north-western Pakistan known mainly from large cemeteries in the middle Swat valley, spreading to Dir, Chitral and Peshawar. The dead were mostly buried, sometimes cremated, in stone-lined graves with pottery and ornaments. Ancient DNA from these graves shows people of Indus-related and steppe-related ancestry mixing in the second millennium BCE.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Painted Grey Ware culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing; known from about 1,500 excavated or surveyed sites and radiocarbon dates; links to the Vedic texts are proposed, not proven.
regions.summary: An Iron Age culture of the western Ganga plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, named after its fine grey pottery painted with black geometric designs. Its people lived in villages and small towns, kept horses, worked ivory and iron, and grew rice, wheat and barley. Many scholars connect it with the later Vedic period and the Kuru and Panchala lands; it gave way to the cities of the Mahajanapadas.
regions.note: No writing; known from about 1,500 excavated or surveyed sites and radiocarbon dates; links to the Vedic texts are proposed, not proven.

regions.name: Iron Age megalithic cultures of South India
regions.evidenceNote: Mostly known from thousands of excavated tombs dated by radiocarbon; Tamil-Brahmi writing appears only near the end.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1200 BCE–200 CE; shown until c. 300 BCE, when the Sangam kingdoms appear on the map
regions.summary: Iron Age peoples of peninsular India who buried their dead, or their bones, in stone-built tombs: dolmens, stone circles, cists and large pottery urns, as at Hire Benakal and Adichanallur. Graves hold iron weapons and tools, black-and-red pottery and beads. These communities of farmers, herders and craftsmen form the background to the early Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam age.
regions.note: Mostly known from thousands of excavated tombs dated by radiocarbon; Tamil-Brahmi writing appears only near the end.
